answer: History, not a forecast. Money set aside for travel and kept in rolling 3-month T-bills roughly held its value in trips. For a trip that is half airfare, half lodging, waiting 10 years cost more (the money bought less of the same trip) in 52.2% of start months from Dec 1997 to Aug 2016, and the median 10-year wait still paid for 99.1% of the trip; the latest 10-year wait (Aug 2016 to Aug 2026) paid for 107.8%. Over 5-year waits, waiting cost more in 45.1% of starts. Airfares alone rose slowly (1.63% a year since late 1997, below T-bills' 2.15%): since 1963, waiting 10 years cost more in 43.2% of starts (median coverage 103.3%). Lodging rose faster (2.38% a year): waiting cost more in 65.2% of starts (median 96.6%).
guess: Retirees often hear that travel prices rise faster than inflation, so they would guess every year of waiting makes the same trips noticeably more expensive than their savings can keep up with.
changesDecision: On prices alone, waiting has been close to a wash: T-bill savings kept pace with airfares more often than not, lagged hotels modestly, and for a mixed trip the median outcome was within one percent of break-even. That removes the price argument from the decision and leaves the reasons that data here cannot measure (health, energy, companions). No advice to travel early or late and no forecast of prices or rates.

assumptions: National price indexes for airline fares and for lodging away from home stand in for the cost of a retiree's trips; actual trips include other costs (cruises, tours, meals, car rental) not measured here.
A 'trip' is fixed at half airfare and half lodging at the start of each window; other mixes give results between the airfare and lodging figures.
The travel fund is kept in 3-month T-bills rolled monthly at the monthly average rate divided by 12 (discount-basis quote, not converted to an investment yield); taxes on interest are ignored.
Price indexes adjust for quality changes and are not seasonally adjusted; booking timing, peak seasons and loyalty discounts are outside the comparison.
limits: History, not a forecast. Lodging data start in Dec 1997, so trip and lodging windows sit mostly in a low-rate period (about three independent 10-year periods); airfare data reach back to 1963. The episode measures only prices against safe savings, not health, which is usually the main reason retirees travel early.
